problems.statement: The 12-hour shift pattern (operator fatigue late in shift) is the cause of the yield decline, as the Plant Manager believes.

Deferred quarterly spindle service (last done May, two deferrals) has allowed bearing wear and runout, which degrades journal size and finish, especially on the tight-tolerance long-shaft machines L3-02 and L3-05.

The Corvane bar change (7.5% saving), and especially the September rise in within-lot hardness scatter after Corvane's billet-source change, increases tool deflection, size scatter and chatter; the in-spec mill certs hide this because they report only hardness means or ranges.

Spindle wear and bar variability are confounded and probably compound: both began in the same week, every lot has run on progressively more worn spindles, and no Line 3 data separates them. A joint cause is more likely than either alone.
The nine new operators with shortened training are the cause of the decline.
The decline is a measurement or inspection artefact (CMM drift, program change, changed reject criteria).

The scrap-tag timing evidence (tags piling up in the last hours of each shift) shows that defects are made late in the shift; in fact it records batch tag-writing at clean-down, so it carries no information on when parts were cut.

Increased manual wear-offset entry and more frequent insert changes on the harder-to-cut bar are a contributing mechanism of size scatter, a downstream effect of bar or spindle condition rather than an independent cause.

The organisational root problem is a decision pattern: cost and delivery pressure produced simultaneous changes (shift pattern, supplier, deferred maintenance, hiring) without controls, change tracking or traceability, plus reliance on certs and a prior anecdote (the 2024 skipped service) to dismiss risks.
Long shifts add secondary harm (fatigue, higher absence, overtime cover) and make maintenance harder to schedule, but are not shown to drive the yield loss.

causalClaims.from: Corvane lot sequence (C-05 to C-10 higher reject rate)

actions.action: Do the deferred spindle service on all six lathes now, two machines at a time on weekend shifts, starting with L3-02 and L3-05, and record runout and vibration before and after.
actions.rationale: It is low cost, shipment risk is now negligible with a 1.2-week backlog, L3-02 and L3-05 are already over the 5 um limit, and a staggered rollout also gives a natural before/after test.

actions.action: Pull CMM results and reject rates for the roughly 1,400 long shafts run on Line 6 with Corvane bar on a serviced spindle, and compare them to L3-02 and L3-05.
actions.rationale: It is the only existing data that partly separates bar from spindle and needs no new production.

actions.action: Take up Tamsworth's two trial lots (about +3% price) and run them on freshly serviced and on unserviced Line 3 machines, with lot and machine traceability.
actions.rationale: A cheap controlled comparison that settles the bar versus spindle question before the supplier decision is locked in.

actions.action: Ask Corvane for hardness and microstructure data on the post-1 September billet source and tighten the incoming spec to include within-lot scatter, not just the range.
actions.rationale: Corvane's own change letter coincides with the larger scatter, and the current acceptance criteria cannot see it.

actions.action: Link CMM serial numbers to lathe cycle-counter logs and record operator and offset entries, so a reject can be traced to machine, time and lot (cycle logs have a 180-day retention, so export them now).
actions.rationale: It stops the next problem being untraceable and allows the shift-fatigue question to be tested properly.

actions.action: Send Halvard a containment plan before the 13 November deadline: keep 100% CMM, add sort or enhanced journal-diameter checks on outbound shafts, and share the investigation plan.
actions.rationale: Customer escapes rose 35 to 290 PPM and the containment deadline has been set.

actions.action: Return Line 3 to 8-hour shifts, but present it as a workload, absence and maintenance-access decision, not as the yield fix, and do it after or staggered with the service so the effects stay separable.
actions.rationale: The backlog is almost cleared and the customer has agreed to 8-hour capacity, but the evidence does not show the shift pattern causes the yield loss.

actions.action: Announce to the plant that the move back to 8-hour shifts will confirm and fix the yield problem.
actions.rationale: If the real causes are spindle wear or bar scatter, yield will not recover, and credibility and time will be lost.

actions.action: Cut Line 3 final CMM inspection from 100% to 1-in-10 sampling.
actions.rationale: Escapes to Halvard are already rising and the inspection system is the only reliable detector; sampling would hide the problem and raise customer PPM.

actions.action: Adopt the Corvane 7.5% saving (about $210,000 per year) as permanent now.
actions.rationale: Scrap and rework already cost about $6,700 per week extra, and the cause of the scatter is unresolved, so wait for the trial lots and the Line 6 data.

actions.action: Retrain or discipline the new operators or reverse the shortened training.
actions.rationale: New and experienced operators have the same reject rates and yield was falling before they ran alone, so this would target the wrong cause.

actions.action: Restore the standing rule that quarterly service is not deferred without a quality and maintenance sign-off, and add a change-control step so that supplier, shift and maintenance changes are not made together on the same line.
actions.rationale: This addresses the organisational pattern that produced multiple confounded changes and the dismissal of warning signs.

nextEvidence: CMM results, reject rates and journal-diameter distributions for the ~1,400 Corvane long shafts run on the serviced Line 6 spare lathe, compared with L3-02 and L3-05 over the same period.
Reject rate by machine before and after spindle service on L3-02 and L3-05 (and then the others), plus Tamsworth trial lot results on serviced and unserviced Line 3 lathes.
Lathe cycle-counter and offset logs matched to CMM serial numbers by time, machine, lot and operator, to test within-shift timing, offset-entry effects and the lot-by-machine interaction.
output.summary: Reverting to 8-hour shifts is unlikely to be the fix. The shift evidence is an artefact: scrap tags are written in a batch at clean-down. Yield began falling in week 32, before the shift change and before any new operator ran alone. New operators reject at the same rate as experienced ones, and the CMM is stable. The live causes are deferred spindle service (runout above limit, rising vibration) and the Corvane bar, whose hardness scatter widened after a billet change. Both started together, so they are confounded and probably compound. Service the spindles now, trial Tamsworth lots, use the Line 6 data, keep 100% inspection, and do not make Corvane permanent yet.
